::: {.decision}
**Your decision.** At yesterday’s close a share traded at HK$100. This morning the firm announces higher earnings. The first post-announcement price is HK$105. A colleague writes, “The market raised its cash-flow forecast by 5%.” Would you sign that sentence?
:::

## Reconstruct the two prices

Imagine a one-year claim with a single future payment and no interim dividends. Use a required return that reflects the risk of this claim. Its price equals the expected payment divided by one plus that return. Yesterday a forecast of HK$110 and a required return of 10% gave 110 / 1.10 = **HK$100**. Two different revisions produce today’s HK$105.

| Account | Expected payment | Required return | Implied price |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Yesterday | 110.00 | 10.00% | 100.00 |
| A. Stronger outlook | 115.50 | 10.00% | 105.00 |
| B. Cheaper capital | 110.00 | 4.76% (rounded) | 105.00 |

Account A might fit a firm that won an unexpected contract. Account B might fit a day when comparable risky claims also rose in price as investors accepted lower returns. Both changes could occur together. The last trade tells us the price at which someone bought and someone sold. One price change cannot identify two revisions.


```{=html}
<figure class="ess-figure" data-essentials-figure="market-prices">
<figcaption><strong>Read two explanations from one price</strong></figcaption>
<p>Each line holds the share price fixed. Points on a line pair an expected one-year payment with a required return.</p>
<div class="ess-chart"></div>
<p><strong>Read the graph.</strong> If the expected payment stays at HK$110, where must the required return move to explain HK$105?</p>
<details><summary>Check your reading</summary><p>Follow the HK$110 level to the HK$105 line. The required return falls to about 4.76%. At the original 10% return, the expected payment would instead need to rise to HK$115.50. The share price alone leaves both explanations open.</p></details>
<noscript><p>Open the explanation for the plotted result.</p></noscript>
</figure>
```

## Read the surprise

Suppose reported earnings rose from HK$8 to HK$9 per share. If the market expected HK$8.50, the surprise was positive. If it expected HK$9.50, the same announcement fell short. Reported earnings describe the period just ended. An analyst still needs to explain why the news changes a future cash flow. An unexpected one-off tax credit and a permanent gain in recurring orders support different revisions.

<details><summary>Try another release before writing the note</summary>
<p>A firm earns HK$10 against a consensus of HK$11 and raises its forecast of next year’s recurring cash flow. The earnings surprise is −HK$1. A price rise is consistent with stronger forward guidance. To assess that account, compare the new guidance with the forecast investors held immediately before the announcement.</p>
</details>

## Write the morning note

“Shares rose 5% around the release. A 5% increase in expected payment would explain the move at yesterday’s required return. To assess that explanation, I would compare timestamped forecast revisions with the price response of similar firms and the change in benchmark yields.” A sector-wide rally would weaken the firm-specific account. Even a narrow event window can contain more than one piece of news.


```{=html}
<section aria-label="Practice brief"><h2>What wording would you clear for the morning note?</h2><details><summary>Compare your recommendation</summary><p>Report the move from HK$100 to HK$105. Before attributing it to higher future earnings, compare guidance with expectations and check whether the required return changed. Either input can explain the price.</p></details></section>
```



```{=html}
<section class="professional-practice" aria-label="Professional route practice"><h2>Apply the graph in practice</h2>
<div data-professional-route="fintech"><p><strong>Markets and fintech.</strong> What should a note say about the move to HK$105 before attributing it to the firm’s outlook?</p><details><summary>Check your recommendation</summary><p>Acknowledge that either stronger expected payments or lower required returns can produce the observed price. Check updated guidance and moves in comparable securities or benchmark yields.</p></details></div>
</section>
```


<details class="full-course-detail"><summary>How much of the move can a rate change explain?</summary><p>Use yesterday’s HK$110 expected payment in both valuations first. At an 8% required return, it would be worth HK$101.85. A price of HK$105 at that same rate implies HK$113.40 of expected payment. This gives one decomposition, conditional on using 8% as the new required return. Use a comparable claim with similar risk and maturity to defend that assumption.</p></details>
